title: The Consequences of Greed
english: You have applied the mind so that it does not surrender the truth out of cowardice, but by winning the difficult criterion through bold speech in the healing of Agrippa, it softens it toward goodness, like beasts watching the handling of the Word.

ariah has prophesied and even now opens the door to us of the great mysteries of the Only-Begotten through the stone, having the sevenfold vision, by means of the golden lampstand, upon which are the seven lamps and the two olive branches (cf. Zech 4). Many of the following Scriptures possess a rich treasure of benefit, to all of which I wished to come and show you the straightness of the spiritual festival.

3.2.3 The promise of the former work hastens me toward the construction of this debt. For having begun to be overwhelmed by many accusations of greed, lest we failed to strip vanity of it, we have set the refutation of the accusation toward the present day. Listen therefore and become discerning judges of the truth, since you judge not by other things, but by your own salvation, and you carry all the condemning votes upon the responsible party, each having driven his own soul away like a house or a city.

d, therefore, is not only to covet silver along with other possessions and to desire to join to what is present that which does not belong, but, to speak more generally, to desire to have more in every matter than what is owed and what is required.

indeed this overflow first suffered the devil, being an archangel and having been appointed over the most excellent life and order, yet conceiving tyranny and rebellion against the Divinity, the fool; then, having been cast down, having fallen into this surrounding air, he became an evil neighbor to our life.

3.3.3 For he did not grasp that which he pursued, the Divinity; and he lost that which he possessed, the archangelhood; an unfaithful slave who, through small acts of audacity, turned into a robber; a dog deprived of the myth and the meat among the Greeks, and having snatched not even the shadow, for how could he grasp an ungraspable thing?

3.3.4 After this, the first man, being enticed by pleasure, lost immortality through forbidden food, just as Esau later lost the firstborn things because of lentil stew (Gen 25:34). And these dialects and the many of the...

A love for more has introduced the voices of men into life. For those having overstepped with human arrogance, expecting to make heaven a path for themselves and making a ridiculous tower upon that vain ascent, they made the same-minded men into foreign-tongued men; and seeking the more which they had, they themselves were continued in this and left the human race to suffer in the hearing of senseless voices and the seeking of interpretations.

What then of Pharaoh? From where did he fall into diverse and varied scourges? Was it not because of greed and the desire to be lord over a foreign people and to not allow anything belonging to that kingdom from anywhere? And because of this, not having released the strangers, he destroyed his own: some in the plague of the firstborn, others in the pursuit by the sea. For I allow rivers to flow into blood, and an immeasurable generation of frogs, and filth of lice, and an outbreak of flies, and the death of the four-footed, and all the evils, by which Egypt was judged because of the greed of the ruler.

But elsewhere again we learned the end of sin: an incurable leprosy poured out upon the greedy one. Remind me also, if anyone is a lover of stories and a friend to the righteous Elisha, how the Syrian Naaman was cleansed of leprosy after washing in the Jordan, but how the disease passed to the child Gehazi, a greedy and unphilosophical youth, having sold the spiritual gift and the free healing of the teacher.

How then did Absalom become a rebel, the son of the gentle father, a flaming and impudent youth? Was it not by seeking the inheritance of the kingdom before the time, leaping upon others as a robber? And Judas, why did he cast out the remnant of the disciples, and instead of an apostle, he made himself a traitor? Was it not first acting as a thief in the treasury, and then the acquisition of dishonorable glory? Why do the Acts lament Ananias and Sapphira among the apostles? Was it not because they became thieves of their own and sacrilegious of the household's devoted things?

Perhaps even today the day will leave off counting the servants of greed. Leaving the old history, let us examine the experience following in life; for greed knows a beast, and whatever it takes, it is always at its peak and not...

title: The Greed of the Sick and the Weather-Watchers
english: Wasting away, joining with those who are sinking and going to an end. , the lover of bodies, even if it rages through desires for a long time, or even having reached priestly age itself or having grown old having seen what is desired and having cast off its bloom, finds a standing place for the disease. The stomach's lust withdraws, either having filled the belly or having become weak from digestive particles and having ceased the heightened appetite. The glory-seeker destroys himself with many flattering appearances of vanity. The disease of greed is an evil that is inseparable; and just   like this ivy, the lush plant and evergreen, it climbs strongly and entwines itself around the trees upon which it intends to cling, and it does not withdraw, neither having suffered nor having dried up, unless someone cuts its coils with iron like a dragon; in this way, it is not easy to free the soul from such a thing, whether the body is being refreshed or having diminished, unless a sober thought comes and like a knife cuts the disease. Hose at home, the greedy man is unpleasant, to servants heavy,   to friends useless, to strangers difficult to deal with, to neighbors a nuisance, to a cohabiting wife a burden, to children stingy and a meager provider, a bad overseer of himself, caring only by night, becoming thick during the day, reasoning with himself according to those who have strayed or are deviating; he is always complaining and groaning as if in need, not enjoying those present and seeking those absent, not using what is his own, but coveting what belongs to others. Flock of such a man is a great burden, narrowing the enclosures   upon which it is penned, covering the pastures in which it grazes; even if a fleshy sheep appears to be approaching, having left his own flock, he approaches with desire toward the one and the other. The same happens with the oxen, similarly with the horses, and no differently with the earth. Everything narrows the house and nothing is useful in use; for the insatiable one is not even enjoyable, but his house is near a tomb. For behold, even tombs are often filled with silver and gold, but the inhabitants do not possess them. The body is not nourished, no profit is found for the soul; for almsgiving does not prosper from the right hand.

What is the end of toil? Let someone warned by such a disease teach this. I know many, having learned through experience, that even in sickness they love money more than health; if a doctor suggests a way of treatment through some substance, such as celery, thyme, or anise, of which supply is inexhaustible, they obey the advice readily; but if some medicine is required that is varied and complex, and they are commanded to go to the druggist or the perfumer, they are more ready to let go of their soul or to loosen their purse. For being earthly, they consider the prudence of possessing earthly goods to be life itself.

These are greatly distressed by common good fortunes, but circumstances bring them joy. They pray that tax-free decrees may come so that they may increase their silver through interest; they desire to see those distressed by lenders, so that they may acquire the field or the vessel or the animal being cast off easily out of necessity. And they constantly look up toward the sky after the philosophers, those attentive to the things in the air, not seeking a command from a star, nor peering to see if any house belongs to one of the planets, but rather attending to the busy state of the air, if the appearing signs promise a flow of rain or hail. Even if they see something difficult approaching for the many, they rejoice in the misfortune of others.

They gather everything into storerooms, marking it securely and fastening it with two locks; they count haphazardly while measuring. And when the greedy one is occupied with such a hope, and finally dreams of becoming rich in the shadow-sketch of ideas, if a deep cloud occurs, he fears it as being dangerous. If light sprinkles the earth, he begins to tear up; but if even rain occurs sufficient to end the hail, it is a matter of complete mourning.

He therefore wanders about, scrutinizing everything regarding the grain as if a son were in danger, asking what shall heal, what machine is needed, so that for a long time it may suffice for many, so that it may escape the blight of the crops. Even if he feels a heat, as doctors have spread him out to differentiate it, he divides and cools himself, settling his toil, a shelter according to the midday.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Perils of Inheritance and the Example of Lazarus
english: He acts like a wise man, stripping away the shadows of night, so that he may be lulled by the night breezes. Poverty stands by this man while he is toiling, seeking from the endangered grain and not giving; or if he does give, he gives grudgingly, and is himself barely covered by a half-measure of grain. Therefore, I urge you, such a person, not to engage in endless toil and hardship.

For both the luxurious covetous man, who limits his life to the stomach and other pleasures, thinking this to be the end of humanity, is worthy of pity. But the small-minded and short-spoken man has no measure of his wretchedness, taking the portion of many and not giving to himself, bringing his haste to nothing.

For who does not know that nothing of the things happening, except virtues, happens by itself, but we do something else in order that we may achieve something else? No one sails more by the act of sailing itself, nor does a farmer live by his labors for the sake of farming alone; but it is evident that both proceed with painful endurance, one to reap the fruitfulness of the earth, the other to carry off the wealth of maritime commerce. And you, say what your end is. Is it to gather things together? And what kind of end is this, to see having heaped up useless matter?

He says, 'The sight even delights me.' Has your own sickness not changed? For it is possible to soothe desire even with the money of others. If the glitter of silver delights you, sitting before the silversmiths, looking at the dense and shining light, or taking pleasure in various vessels, both those that carry food and those that pour; for the sight is easy and unhindered for you.

See also the silver-experts at the tables, constantly feeling and counting the coins; rather, I will advise you: change your mind through something good. For correction is easy, since greed is not a necessity of nature, but an impulse of choice, which is not difficult to change for those choosing what is profitable.

Peer with your thought into the time hereafter, when you will not be, when a little earth will lie over you, your body folded up and senseless; and a few flakes of ash will cover the remains. Where then will the wealth and the gathered treasures be? Who will be the heir of those left behind? For not all...

That person will be the successor you expect. If you leave children, they might happen to stumble, and a greedy person like you might drive them away from the father's house while they are mourning. Even if you are poor and send the inheritance to some friends, do not treat the will as an unshakeable law, as an irrefutable and strong thing. A little haste makes the writing void. Do you not see those constantly struggling in the courts against wills, where lawyers lead various schemes, bringing in legal experts to strike against them, bringing in terrible rhetoricians as helpers, nurturing false witnesses, and corrupting the courts?

For this reason, regarding those things you see happening, instruct those who come after you. If you have wealth justly, use it properly, like the blessed Job; if unjustly, distribute it to those who were plundered, like a prisoner of war; or take what you received along with an addition, like Zacchaeus. If you do not have it, do not acquire it wickedly. For sin will follow you as a bitter provision on a necessary journey, and the enjoyment of what was acquired will be left to those you do not know. Then you will marvel at David saying, 'He stores up, but does not know to whom he will gather it' (Ps 69:8). And you will know the rich man, the opposite of Lazarus, who has been fully read to us from the Gospels, not composed as a myth for astonishment, but handed down as an exact type of what is to come.

The deep has been spread out, the kingdom has passed to another, the luxuries have been abolished; sin from those things has emigrated along with them like a shadow remaining to a walking body. And because of this, after the luxury of banquets and the elegant table, a thin drop of water is sought, departing from a finger thin from disease; and he calls the poor man the healer of punishment, who perhaps does not even have hands when he rushes to the gate; for he would have driven away the dogs that were licking the wounds.
